summary: Return the k-th largest element of an unsorted array (not necessarily distinct).
mainInsight: You do not need a full sort: keep only the k largest seen so far in a size-k min-heap. Its root is the smallest of those k, so it is both the next one to evict and, at the end, the k-th largest. That gives O(n log k); quickselect improves the average to O(n).

approaches.name: Min-heap of size k
approaches.summary: Keep the k largest; the root is the answer.
approaches.interviewRelevance: The expected answer; mention quickselect as the O(n) average-time follow-up.

approaches.name: Quickselect
approaches.summary: Partition around a pivot, recursing into one side.
approaches.interviewRelevance: The follow-up: best average time, but know the O(n^2) worst case and that it mutates the input.

approaches.name: Counting array over the value range
approaches.summary: Count occurrences per value and walk from the largest.
strengths: Linear when the range R is small
approaches.interviewRelevance: Your approach: valid under the constraints.

personalSolution.approach: Counting array over the value range
personalSolution.notes: Valid because values are bounded. In general use a size-k min-heap (O(n log k)), the expected interview answer, or quickselect (O(n) average).

promptVariants: Which structure keeps only the k largest elements seen so far?
What do you maintain while scanning to avoid sorting for the k-th largest?
options: Queue holding the last k items
cards.explanation: The smallest of the kept elements sits at the root, so it is the one to evict when a larger element arrives.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Max-heap capped at size k: Its root is the largest, so evicting it throws away the best candidate.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Monotonic stack of size k: A monotonic stack tracks next-greater relations, not the k largest values overall.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Queue holding the last k items: That keeps the most recent k elements, not the largest k.

promptVariants: Why a min-heap and not a max-heap for the k largest, and why is the root the answer?
Why is the root of a size-k min-heap of the largest values the k-th largest?
cards.answer: The heap holds the k largest seen so far. A min-heap puts the smallest of them at the root, which is exactly the one to evict when a bigger element arrives. After all elements, the root is the smallest of the top k, i.e. the k-th largest.
keyPoints: Min-heap: root is the smallest of the kept k, so it is the eviction candidate
Pop when size exceeds k, so the heap always holds the k largest
Final root = smallest of the top k = k-th largest
cards.explanation: A max-heap would put the largest element at the root, which is the one you want to keep.

promptVariants: Trace nums = [7,4,9,2,8], k = 3 through this code: what does the heap hold after each element, and what is returned?
Walk this heap solution on [7,4,9,2,8] with k = 3. What is popped at each step?
cards.code:
import heapq

heap = []
for num in nums:
    heapq.heappush(heap, num)
    if len(heap) > k:
        heapq.heappop(heap)
return heap[0]
cards.answer: After 7: {7}. After 4: {4,7}. After 9: {4,7,9}. After 2: push 2, size 4 > 3, pop 2, so {4,7,9}. After 8: push 8, pop 4, so {7,8,9}. The root is the smallest of {7,8,9}, so 7 is returned.
keyPoints: Pop removes the smallest, so the heap always holds the k largest so far
Elements smaller than everything kept are pushed and popped straight away
Return heap[0], the smallest of the top k
cards.explanation: heappop always removes the minimum, which is why the heap converges to the k largest values.

promptVariants: Time complexity of the size-k min-heap solution for n elements: ___
Scanning n elements with a heap capped at size k takes ___.
cards.explanation: n elements, each with one push and at most one pop on a heap of size at most k + 1, so O(log k) each.

promptVariants: Extra space of the size-k min-heap solution: ___
How much memory does a heap capped at size k use? ___
cards.explanation: The heap never holds more than k + 1 elements, regardless of n.

promptVariants: When would you choose the heap over quickselect, and quickselect over the heap?
The interviewer asks for better than O(n log k). What do you offer and what do you give up?
cards.answer: Quickselect is O(n) on average versus O(n log k) for the heap, but its worst case is O(n^2) and it mutates the input. The heap has a guaranteed bound, leaves the input alone and works on a stream; for small k its O(n log k) is close to linear anyway.
keyPoints: Quickselect O(n) average, O(n^2) worst case
Quickselect mutates the input; heap does not
Heap has a guaranteed bound and works on streams
cards.explanation: Lead with the heap, then offer quickselect as the average-case optimisation and name its trade-offs.

promptVariants: Walk through the descending scan `k -= arr[i]; if k <= 0: return i + low` and explain the offset `low`.
Why does the scan return the k-th largest including duplicates?
cards.answer: Counts are stored at index value - low so negatives fit. Scanning from the largest value downward, subtracting each value's count from k counts how many elements are >= the current value; when k reaches 0 or below, the k-th largest (counting duplicates) lies at this value, which is i + low.
keyPoints: Walk values from largest to smallest

promptVariants: What is the 2nd largest of [9,4,9,7,1]?
Do duplicates count separately? What is the 2nd largest of [9,4,9,7,1]?
cards.explanation: Sorted descending: 9, 9, 7, 4, 1, so the 2nd largest element (duplicates count separately) is 9; counting distinct values would give 7.

incorrectOptionExplanations.7: 7 is the 2nd largest distinct value; the problem counts elements, not distinct values.

promptVariants: Why is the k-th largest equal to the root of a size-k min-heap of the largest values?
Why does a counting array work in your solution and when does it not?
cards.answer: A size-k min-heap keeps the k largest seen; its root is the smallest of them, which is exactly the k-th largest. Your counting array works because the value range is bounded (about 2*10^4 wide), so counts can be scanned from the top; with a huge range the array would be too large.

promptVariants: Average time of quickselect: ___
Finding the k-th largest by partitioning takes ___ on average.
cards.explanation: Each partition halves the expected remaining work.

promptVariants: What is the space cost of your counting-array solution and of the heap solution?
Compare the memory of counting vs heap vs quickselect.
cards.answer: Counting: O(R) where R = max - min + 1. Heap: O(k). Quickselect: O(1) extra (in place) with O(log n) recursion if recursive.
cards.explanation: R must be bounded for counting.
